We discussed whether or not patents should be abolished in my class today after listening to this planet money podcast. It brought up an interesting question as patents can be useful to encourage investment in new technologies however patent holders can also use them against anybody who wants to improve the product or industry. I'm kind of torn on what to think here.

Patent trolling should be.

"Patent trolling" is actually a complicated issue. I know a few people who work in intellectual property, and they say that a lot of people who would be caught by anti-"patent troll" legislation are poor inventors who are ignored by manufacturing companies, and therefore unable to utilize their patent effectively, but still should absolutely keep the rights to their ideas. They claim it's not too rare to simply see someone's ideas taken, and then have them be labelled a "patent troll" when they attempt to collect on people who utilize their patented ideas.

As far as people who buy patents with the express intent of "trolling," they'll usually just say that, in the end, it comes down to the fact that the party did buy the rights to that patent, so if another party is using the contents of that patent, then they have every right to some of that party's profits. Their stance seems to be that, for better or worse, even "patent trolls" are entitled to the fruits of any intellectual property they own.

You provide two good examples, but I think it should be fairly easy to distinguish between the two - In one case, someone is working hard to design a product or small subset of products, but they likely wouldn't own a large portfolio of patents.

On the flip side, a patent troll will usually have a large number of patents, more than they could hope to develop within the patent time spans.

Also, you should be able to easily tell if someone has filed a large number of patent lawsuits every time they think their patent has been used vs someone who is actually defending intellectual rights, which would usually be a little more specific and limited in scope.

Look at it this way. If you went to the trouble inventing something wouldn't you expect to get something for it? Also who's going to bother at all if there's nothing in it for them? Technology comes to stand still.

This comment is exactly why patents exist. However, your class discussion raises valid points as well, which is why patents don't last forever - They're designed to last long enough for the researchers to recuperate their investment + profit from it. The idea is once it has been in the market long enough, it becomes available for everyone to build upon.

Of course corporations, governments, and all sorts of other leechers see opportunity to abuse the system and earn some quick cash. So they try to do so any chance they get, which is why patents often have a negative connotation attached to them.

As someone who has had to fight patent trolls, I have to wholeheartedly disagree with you.

You don't need to invent anything to get a patent--you just have to come up with an idea. You don't need to prove that your idea will work, that it makes sense, or even make a working model of your idea to get a patent.

The current patent system in the United States is broken and doesn't benefit inventors.

If you had $10K and were bored, you could get a patent by going to a lawyer and telling him to fill out the paperwork for a patent for any damn fool idea you want; for instance, you could say, " I would like to patent shoes that charge your cell phone when you walk".

Then, imagine that a few years later, someone goes and builds shoes that charge your cell phone when you walk; only that first person had already patented the idea... The person who actually built the shoes, and contributed to society, gets nothing.
I don't disagree the way it is currently implemented doesn't work 100%, which is why there is a 2nd paragraph in my comment. I'm sure you noticed I wasn't referring to specific laws, nor was OP.
How often does that even happen? Sounds odd

All the time. Big companies have employees where that's their entire job.

This got a little better in 2000 after they closed up the "submarine patent" loophole, but that just caused the mentality to shift. The current philosophy is just patent anything and everything.

Eliminating patents allows consumers to get better products by encouraging competition and letting anyone use whatever the best inventions in existence are. Also companies can just try to be "first on the market" with their technology as their incentive to innovate. This will make innovation happen a lot quicker and it takes some degree of time and effort just to copy them. If anything patents discourage innovation by creating monopolies.

I'd limit patents and copyright to 5-10 years with no option for renewal. Patents applications would have to demonstrate non-trivial research and a working proof-of-concept implemention before being accepted.

Ideas are nothing. Execution is everything. If an idea is really that valuable, five years of monopoly over it should provide plenty of incentive. Elsewise, people should focus on incremental improvements--where IP monopolies actually get in the way.

I'm about to open a business and I would like a patent. I'm going to get one once I finish working on it more.

Patents are great for the little guys.

There wouldnt be any issue with patents (or copyrights) if they had a hard deadline for expiration after a reasonably short period of time, say 5-10 years or so. A patent is intended to allow an inventor to recuperate a portion of their investment. It needs to exist for that reason, but it also needs to expire so that it doesn't stifle technological growth.

Copyrights are also an issue. In america, copyrights from the 1920's are still active in some cases (you can thank mickey mouse for that)

I think one fundamental problem with patents, that's never mentioned, is that people often independently develop the same idea around the same time. This is a well known phenomena known as Multiple Discovery. The most typical example is calculus. An abstract and complex mathematical methodology was near simultaneously discovered by two people with no connection to one another. And that was at a time when the educated population was numerically an infinitesimal fraction of what it is today. To say nothing of the internet giving people access to vast amounts of information to help in the development of their ideas.

Another problem with patents is that they are not readily available to protect independent inventors or even smaller companies in some instances. This is a list of the hundreds of fees that may be involved in setting up a patent. At the high end they reach $18,000. And there is also no guarantee your work is actually protected. Patents, even once granted, can be overturned and nullified. There are millions of patents filed per year and ensuring you don't run into conflict with another patent or some other form of prior art is on you. Even if you pay the patent office to perform a search (which is hundreds to thousands of dollars) and they find no conflicts that doesn't mean there are none and their failed search does not indemnify you in any way.

I think the patent system should be abolished but not the ethos of patents. Right now if I was an author I could post a book I'd written on here and you could not copy it and sell it, or claim it as your own. This is because copyright is implicitly granted. This is also true, quite to the annoyance of many people, with code. As a professional developer I cannot simply copy/use code somebody intended other people to use if he does not attach a license to it. I think the same should be true of patents with the standard of proof similar to civil court - a preponderance of evidence. I wonder how much the patent system, as it currently exists, actually serves the purpose of patents. For instance Apple and Samsung bickering over whether their tablets, which are hardly a novel idea, esoterically infringe upon some patent or another is just silly and is used more as a business tactic than to actually provide protection for anything new. Patents should protect clear and substantially new ideas, not allow companies to try to get competitive advantages from old ideas.

I think the issue isn't patents themselves, but how we deal with demonstrably frivolous lawsuits. If a patent suit is proven to be nonsense, the defendant should be awarded compensation for legal fees automatically. Reinvention needs to be rewarded, not penalized.

Of course, I think patents shouldn't work the same at all in the medical industry. Medical patents, whether it's a new cure or a new needle design, a treatment or a goddamn band-aid, the patent should not guarantee exclusivity of manufacturing. It should only guarantee royalty rates of say 6% of profits (par for the course in IP royalties). It's one thing when it's a chair or a car, but if it saves lives, there's gotta be a different set of rules.

Definitely get rid of patents entirely. It's nothing more than monopoly and just because you invented something doesn't mean you're entitled to be the only one who can make money off of that kind of product. Even if you invented it, if you can't compete with the people copying you you shouldn't be in business. Also it means better and cheaper products for consumers when there's more competition and anyone can make anything using any technology.

Also with the rate at which technology is moving it makes enough sense to just make everyone try to innovate faster than they can be copied.
In general no but there should be more exceptions like medicine and patens should expire faster

Aircraft reciprocating engines have used dual spark plugs and dual ignition systems for ever. For the pre-take off engine check you run the engine up to about 1200 RPM and shutdown one mag and watch the RPM drop. Then you bring both mags back on line and watch the RPM increase. Then you shut down the other mag and watch the RPM drop. Both mags being cut out should yield about a 50-100 RPM Drop with no rough running. In Aircraft reciprocating engines dual plugs and ignitions systems are for power and not for Safety. However it's nice to know that if you lose a plug the results won't be disastrous.
